title: Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) Extension to Establish Keys for the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP)
summary: Describes a DTLS extension to establish keys for SRTP and SRTCP flows. The keying happens on the media path, independent of any out-of-band signaling. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: To scramble a video call, both sides need a shared secret. This extension lets the two devices agree on it directly over the call's own connection.

questions: how are srtp keys established with dtls
how does dtls-srtp tell dtls from rtp packets
which srtp protection profiles does rfc 5764 define
subtitle: How two endpoints use a DTLS handshake on the media path to get the keys that protect their SRTP audio and video.

tldr.problem: SRTP protects RTP media but has no key management of its own, so it depends on some external way to exchange master keys and negotiate algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: The peers run a DTLS handshake on the same ports as the media, negotiate SRTP with a use_srtp extension, and export the SRTP master keys and salts from the DTLS session using a TLS exporter.
tldr.outcome: Keying happens on the media path, independent of any out-of-band signalling. Media is then sent as ordinary SRTP packets with no DTLS framing, which has to be told apart from DTLS and STUN packets by looking at the first byte.

today: RFC 5764 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 7983 and RFC 9443. Check those documents for changes to the details described here, such as how packets on the shared port are told apart.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Secure RTP profile (SRTP, RFC 3711) can give RTP and RTCP traffic confidentiality, message authentication and replay protection. But SRTP provides no key management. It depends on something external to exchange secret master keys and to negotiate the algorithms and parameters used with them.

Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS, RFC 4347) has integrated key management, parameter negotiation and data transfer, but its data transfer is generic and less tuned for RTP than SRTP is. DTLS-SRTP combines the two: it keeps the performance and encryption flexibility of SRTP and adds the convenience of DTLS-integrated key and association management. It can be seen as a new key management method for SRTP, or as a new RTP-specific data format for DTLS.

The key points are that application data is protected with SRTP, the DTLS handshake establishes the keying material, algorithms and parameters, a DTLS extension negotiates the SRTP algorithms, and other DTLS record types still use the ordinary DTLS record format.
sections.eli5: SRTP is a good lock for video calls but it has no way to hand out keys. DTLS is good at handing out keys. This memo makes them team up: DTLS hands over the key, SRTP does the locking.

sections.title: How a DTLS-SRTP Session Is Laid Out
sections.content:
DTLS-SRTP is defined for point-to-point sessions with exactly two participants. Each session has one DTLS association and either two SRTP contexts (media flows both ways) or one (media flows one way). A session protects data on a single UDP source and destination port pair. Which side is the DTLS client and which is the server must be decided out of band, for example with SDP.

RTP and RTCP usually travel on two separate UDP ports. With symmetric RTP (RFC 4961), two bidirectional DTLS-SRTP sessions are needed, one for RTP and one for RTCP. Without it, four unidirectional ones are needed. If RTP and RTCP are multiplexed on one port (RFC 5761), the number of sessions is halved. Between one pair of participants there MUST be a separate DTLS-SRTP session for each distinct pair of ports used by a media session, although the sessions can share one DTLS session.

An implementation SHOULD set up a single DTLS association first and let the others wait, so the later handshakes can use DTLS session resumption and spread the cost of the public key operations. The client and server use different SRTP keys for the packets they send, and the SRTP implementation MUST make sure that the SSRC values of all sources on one device and channel are distinct, to avoid the "two-time pad" problem.

When the signalling is integrity-protected, for example with SIP Identity, DTLS-SRTP can build on it to secure the whole media stream. RFC 5763 describes how to indicate DTLS-SRTP in SIP and SDP and how to authenticate endpoints with fingerprints.
sections.eli5: Two people on a call each get their own set of keys, one for what they say and one for what they hear. Each separate stream of video or audio gets its own tunnel, but they can share the first meeting to save time.

sections.title: The use_srtp Extension and Protection Profiles
sections.content:
A client asks for SRTP by adding a use_srtp extension to its DTLS hello. The extension MUST only be used when the data is RTP or RTCP. It carries a list of acceptable SRTP protection profiles in descending order of preference, plus an optional srtp_mki value of up to 255 bytes (zero length means no MKI). A server that accepts answers with its own use_srtp extension naming a single profile, which MUST be one the client offered. If there is no shared profile, the server SHOULD NOT return the extension, and the connection falls back to the negotiated DTLS cipher suite; if that is unacceptable the server SHOULD send an alert.

Four profiles are defined: SRTP_AES128_CM_HMAC_SHA1_80 (0x00, 0x01), SRTP_AES128_CM_HMAC_SHA1_32 (0x00, 0x02), SRTP_NULL_HMAC_SHA1_80 (0x00, 0x05) and SRTP_NULL_HMAC_SHA1_32 (0x00, 0x06). The key derivation rate is zero, so keys are not re-derived from the SRTP sequence number, and the SRTP defaults apply to the rest. Applications SHOULD coordinate profiles between the RTP and RTCP sessions, and identical ciphers SHOULD be used.

The Master Key Identifier (MKI) tells an SRTP receiver which key protected a packet. The client MUST pick an MKI that differs from the last one it used. The server either echoes a matching MKI or returns an empty one to say it cannot use MKIs. If the client sees a different nonzero MKI in the reply, it MUST abort the handshake and SHOULD send an invalid_parameter alert.
sections.eli5: The caller hands over a list of lock types it can use, best first. The other side picks one from that list. If nothing matches, they fall back to ordinary DTLS protection.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Key Limits
sections.content:
SRTP packets and ordinary DTLS records use different keys. The SRTP keys come from a TLS exporter (RFC 5705) with the label EXTRACTOR-dtls_srtp and an empty context. It produces 2 * (master_key_len + master_salt_len) bytes, split into a client write master key, a server write master key, a client write master salt and a server write master salt.

The client key and salt feed one invocation of the SRTP key derivation function to make the keys for packets the client sends. The server key and salt do the same for the server. A receiver MUST only use the other side's keys to decrypt and check inbound packets. When RTP and RTCP use different ports, there are two DTLS-SRTP sessions, and each one throws away the keys for the protocol it does not carry.

Each profile has a maximum_lifetime of 2^31 packets per set of keys, with RTP and RTCP counted separately. When it is reached, a new DTLS session SHOULD be used for replacement keys, and the old keys MUST NOT be used for outbound or inbound traffic. Because packets can be reordered, implementations SHOULD keep several key sets during a rekey.
sections.eli5: The secret from the handshake is stirred into four numbers: two for each person, one for locking and one for mixing. Each direction of the call uses its own set, and a key that has been used too many times has to be replaced.

sections.title: Sending and Receiving Protected Media
sections.content:
Once use_srtp is negotiated, RTP and RTCP are protected only by SRTP and never sent as DTLS application_data records. The application hands a packet to DTLS as an ordinary write, DTLS applies the RFC 3711 processing, and the resulting SRTP packet goes on the wire as a single datagram with no DTLS framing. The RTP sequence number is used, not a DTLS one. SRTP processing MUST NOT begin before the handshake completes. Non-RTP data, such as TLS control messages, uses ordinary DTLS framing and MUST be in separate datagrams.

Because DTLS, SRTP and STUN (RFC 5389) packets can arrive on the same port, the receiver reads the first byte: 0 or 1 means STUN, 20 to 63 means DTLS, and 128 to 191 means RTP (or RTCP when multiplexed).

When one local port has several DTLS-SRTP associations, for example after SIP forking, RTP cannot tell them apart from the source address. The receiver keeps a table of SSRC to association. A known SSRC uses its association. An unknown SSRC is tried against each association; if the authentication tag verifies, the SSRC is added to the table, and otherwise the packet is silently discarded. Entries MUST be removed when an association closes. Receivers MAY give up on SSRCs that keep failing, and such entries SHOULD time out faster than the call, with 10 to 30 seconds suggested.
sections.eli5: Video packets go out in their own sealed envelopes with no extra wrapper. The receiver looks at the first byte of each packet, like a sticker on the envelope, to see whether it is a call packet, a handshake packet or a network helper packet.

sections.title: Rekeying and Multi-Party Sessions
sections.content:
Rekeying is a new DTLS handshake over the existing channel, protected by the current cipher suite and run in parallel with the media, so the data flow need not stop. When it finishes, the new keys protect all outbound packets. Receivers SHOULD keep both key sets for a while, for the maximum segment lifetime, because older packets may still arrive. If an MKI is in use the matching key set is used, and a packet with no matching MKI MUST be rejected. Without an MKI, the receiver SHOULD try the new keys first, and MAY fall back to the old keys if authentication fails; a packet that fails both MUST be discarded.

DTLS is point-to-point, so DTLS-SRTP is meant only for unicast RTP sessions. It can still be used with RTP mixers, for instance a conference bridge securing each participant's flow, but each flow has its own key, so the mixer must decrypt and re-encrypt traffic for every recipient. The RFC says a future specification might describe sharing one key between associations.
sections.eli5: To change the lock mid-call, the two sides quietly agree on a new key while talking, then switch. For a short while they keep the old key handy in case a late packet shows up.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Negotiation. An attacker might try to force plain DTLS instead of SRTP. Because the extension is negotiated inside the handshake, the Finished messages protect it, so such a bid-down attack is detected and becomes a denial of service by anyone who controls the channel.

Framing confusion. Two framings share one channel, so an attacker might try to pass an SRTP packet off as a DTLS record or the reverse. Different MAC keys are used for each type, so this reduces to forging a valid MAC. The DTLS record type is also included in the MAC, so an SRTP record would be treated as an unknown type and ignored.

Sequence numbers and trying several keys. The SRTP and DTLS sequence number spaces are distinct, so DTLS control records cannot be ordered against SRTP packets. Implementations that use alerts MUST check for alert retransmission and discard retransmitted alerts. Trying several key sets without an MKI weakens an n-bit MAC by log_2(k) bits for k key sets, which the RFC calls minimal since k is very small and the SRTP default MAC is 80 bits.

Decryption cost. An attacker can send superficially valid SRTP packets that force extra decryptions. The RFC calls this modest, and says one 1024-bit RSA private key operation is hundreds of times as expensive as decrypting an SRTP packet. Under attack, implementations SHOULD prioritize packets with known SSRCs or from known peer addresses.
sections.eli5: Tricking the call into using weaker protection gets noticed, so the worst a bad guy can do is break the call. Mixing up the two kinds of packets does not work either, because each kind has its own secret stamp.

sections.title: SDP Tokens and IANA Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC defines new SDP proto tokens. For RTP/SAVP or RTP/SAVPF over DTLS with UDP they are UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVP and UDP/TLS/RTP/SAVPF. Over DTLS with DCCP they are DCCP/TLS/RTP/SAVP and DCCP/TLS/RTP/SAVPF. How to use offer/answer with DTLS-SRTP is left to RFC 5763.

The RFC adds use_srtp (14) as a DTLS extension type, which MUST only be used with DTLS and not TLS. IANA created a DTLS SRTPProtectionProfile registry, with new values allocated by the Specification Required policy, and registered the EXTRACTOR-dtls_srtp label. The RFC does not cover protecting RTP over TCP and says a new document would be needed for that.
sections.eli5: New names were added to the official lists so that call setup messages can say "this call uses DTLS-SRTP", and the secret-key label and the lock type numbers were written down in public registries.
